llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan:  School Desegregation and Housing Prices in Charlotte–Mecklenburg  

====================================================================

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study in a two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) framework.  

Justification  
• The 1971 court order (Swann v. CMS) was abrupt, externally imposed, and applied district-wide, but neighborhoods differed ex-ante in how much the plan changed the racial/quality mix of their assigned schools.  
• We observe multiple years before and after the shock, allowing a DID with neighborhood and year fixed effects and an event-time specification to test for pre-trends.  
• An event-study yields dynamic treatment effects; the DID coefficient is the average post-policy effect.  
• Other designs (RDD, IV) are less attractive: there is no clear running variable with a sharp cutoff, and the policy date is common to all units, so time-series discontinuity has too little power.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for neighborhoods whose assigned elementary school experienced a large mechanically induced racial re-composition—operationally, those above the median predicted increase in Black-white exposure caused by the busing plan.  
Continuous version:  ΔIntegration_i = forecasted ∆(Black share × White share) 1971–72.

Control group  
Neighborhoods whose assigned school saw minimal predicted change (bottom quartile of ΔIntegration_i). They provide the counterfactual evolution of housing prices absent a salient desegregation shock.

Treatment timing / event date  
t = 0 is school year 1971–72 (September 1971). We code Post_t = 1 for sales dated September 1971 or later.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Parallel pre-trends:  Absent the court order, treated and control neighborhoods would have had similar housing-price trajectories.  
   • Plausibility: Charlotte had unified tax and school governance; no concurrent housing policy shock is recorded. Testable via event-study coefficients for k = -4,…,-1.  

A2. No differential time-varying confounders:  Other shocks (e.g., highway openings) are not systematically correlated with treatment intensity.  
   • Plausibility: Use neighborhood-specific time trends and control for distance to new highways.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA):  Minimal spillovers across neighborhoods.  
   • Plausibility: Some spillover is possible through mobility; we will test for spillovers by excluding ½-mile buffers around treated areas.

A4. Exogeneity of treatment intensity:  ΔIntegration_i is mechanically generated by court-ordered re-zoning, not by housing-market choices.  
   • Plausibility: Plans were designed by the district using racial maps, not negotiated with homeowners.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  

T1. Anticipation / information leaks  
   • Mitigation: Drop sales within 9 months before the plan announcement (January–August 1971) and test for price movements in 1970.  

T2. Residential sorting after the shock  
   • Mitigation: (i) restrict sample to repeat-sales or hedonic indices that difference out property fixed effects; (ii) re-estimate using only sales of pre-1968 structure vintages to reduce endogenous building.  

T3. Time-varying school quality improvements unrelated to integration (new principals, Title I dollars)  
   • Mitigation: Control for observable school-input changes (teacher-student ratio, per-pupil spending). Use school fixed effects interacted with time to absorb idiosyncratic quality shocks.

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # TWFE and event studies
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
house   <- fread("housing_transactions_CMS.csv")      # price-level data
schools <- fread("school_characteristics_CMS.csv")    # quality + racial mix
cz_map  <- fread("neigh_school_link.csv")             # neighborhood⇄school mapping
demo    <- fread("census_neighborhood_demo.csv")

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
## Merge
setkey(house, neighborhood_id);  setkey(demo, neighborhood_id)
dat <- merge(house, demo, by = "neighborhood_id")
dat <- merge(dat, cz_map, by = "neighborhood_id")
dat <- merge(dat, schools[,.(school_id, year, black_share, test_scores,
                             ppspend)], 
             by.x = c("school_id","sale_year"), 
             by.y = c("school_id","year"), all.x = TRUE)

## Treatment intensity (pre-computed outside or do quick within-R)
delta_int <- fread("predicted_integration_shock.csv")   # ΔIntegration_i per neighborhood
dat <- merge(dat, delta_int, by = "neighborhood_id")

## Treated dummy
median_shock <- median(delta_int$delta_integration)
dat[, treated := (delta_integration >= median_shock)]
dat[, post := sale_year >= 1971 & sale_month >= 9]

## Event time k = sale_year - 1971 (adjust month for precision)
dat[, event_time := sale_year - 1971]
dat[event_time == 0 & sale_month < 9, event_time := -1]   # before Sept 1971 -> still ‑1
for(k in -5:5) dat[, paste0("event_",k) := as.numeric(event_time==k)]

## Outcome
dat[, ln_price := log(sale_price)]

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID regression
did_main <- feols(ln_price ~ treated*post + 
                    beds + baths + sqft + year_built +
                    delta_integration*post +     # continuous intensity
                    i(sale_year) + i(neighborhood_id), 
                  data = dat, cluster = ~neighborhood_id)
summary(did_main)

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study specification
es <- feols(ln_price ~ i(event_time, treated, ref=-1) + 
              beds + baths + sqft + year_built +
              i(neighborhood_id) + i(sale_year), 
            data = dat[abs(event_time)<=5], cluster = ~neighborhood_id)
iplot(es, xlab="Years relative to desegregation", 
          ylab="ln(price) difference Treated-Control")

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: buffer-zone drop
dat_rb <- dat[distance_to_treated > 0.5]  # drop close neighbors (miles)
did_rb <- update(did_main, data = dat_rb)
etable(list(Main=did_main, BufferRemoved=did_rb))
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Theory:  A sudden increase in racial integration was perceived by a subset of white homebuyers as a (subjective) decline in school quality, while Black families may value proximity to integrated schools. Charlotte’s overall housing market was majority-white at the time, so the net capitalization likely tilts negative.  

Prior: Treated neighborhoods will experience a 2 – 5 percent decline in log housing prices (≈ 0.02 – 0.05 log points) in the first two post-policy years, fading thereafter as the district’s reputation for successful desegregation grew.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
C1 Pre-trends visually flat in event study………..1  
C2 No contemporaneous confounders……………….0.5  
C3 No anticipation (sales suppressed pre-shock)…0.5  
C4 Stable composition / limited sorting……………0  
C5 Correct functional form & clustered SEs………1  

Total = 3/5. Plenty of room for further robustness (migration modeling, boundary designs, IV for ΔIntegration).
